title: Trigger.dev: Open-Source Workflow Orchestration Guide
summary: Trigger.dev now offers durable AI agents that preserve state across failures.
body_markdown:
## How to connect trigger.dev to an Activepieces workflow today


**There is no native support** : Activepieces, the MIT-licensed flow builder many automation teams already use for triggers, app steps and AI steps, has shipped nothing specific to trigger.dev.


A check of its repository and integration catalog on 2 November 2026 found no trigger.dev integration. Three generic routes remain. None has been tested for this article.


Start at the top of the list below and move down only when the simpler route can't do the job. It ranks the routes by how little setup each needs.


1. An HTTP request step that calls the trigger.dev API with a Bearer secret key.
2. An AI step using any major model or your own provider key.
3. A connection to an MCP server.


The further down you go, the more of the integration you take on yourself, and the sections below say where.


### How to call Trigger.dev with an HTTP request


Activepieces flows connect to other systems through integrations, and a run costs 1 credit however many steps it has, so the extra call doesn't change the bill.


Point it at the trigger.dev API, send the secret key as a Bearer token, and start a task from the flow.


Keep the key in a stored connection rather than typed into the step, or anyone who can edit the flow can read it.


The cost is that you own the result handling: the request starts the work, but your flow still needs a way to learn when long-running work finishes.


On the second route, Activepieces AI steps work with any major model or your own provider key, and when you bring your own AI keys on the Plus plan ($20 a month) each AI step costs 1 credit, so your monthly credit budget directly limits your step count.


This route only helps if something that answers as a model sits in front of your trigger.dev work, and that endpoint is code your team would write and host.


We found nothing from trigger.dev that provides one, so treat this as a build decision.


With an MCP server connection, a model in the flow can call tools instead of you wiring each request by hand. It gives the most flexibility and the least certainty.


What the model can do depends on the tools the server exposes, so list them in your pilot before you promise anything.


Activepieces needs no second catalog for this route.


The 746 integrations counted in packages/integrations/community of the MIT-licensed repo are each written as a integration, and the integration action that runs as a flow step is the same one a per-project MCP server exposes as a tool to Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor or an agent you built.


The Integrations Framework and MCP Server documentation describe that mechanism, so an HTTP step you set up for trigger.dev can become something an agent calls without being wired twice.
